interactions.label: Which of the following features best distinguishes dysentery from diarrhoea?

params.question: Which of the following features best distinguishes dysentery from diarrhoea?

answers.text: Passage of three or more loose stools per day

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the WHO definition of diarrhoea itself, not what distinguishes dysentery. Diarrhoea refers to increased frequency of loose or liquid stools due to secretory or absorptive dysfunction.

answers.text: Presence of blood and mucus in stool with tenesmus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Dysentery is specifically defined as diarrhoea accompanied by blood and mucus, with tenesmus (painful straining), indicating mucosal invasion and inflammation — the hallmark of invasive enteric infection.

answers.text: Short incubation period with multiple persons affected from a common source

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern — rapid onset from a shared exposure — is characteristic of food poisoning, not dysentery. Food poisoning results from ingesting preformed toxins or pathogens from contaminated food.
Large-volume watery stools without blood are characteristic of secretory diarrhoea (e.g., cholera). Dysentery typically produces small-volume bloody mucoid stools due to colonic mucosal invasion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Dysentery is defined by blood and mucus in the stool with tenesmus, reflecting mucosal invasion — unlike secretory diarrhoea (watery, large-volume) or food poisoning (short incubation, common source).
Well done! Dysentery = invasive (blood + mucus + tenesmus), versus diarrhoea which is secretory (watery, large-volume, no blood).

params.question: Why does reheating cream pastries to boiling NOT prevent Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning?

answers.text: S. aureus forms heat-resistant endospores that survive boiling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: S. aureus does NOT form endospores — that is a property of Bacillus and Clostridium species. The heat resistance in staphylococcal food poisoning is due to the preformed toxin, not the organism itself.

answers.text: Reheating promotes further toxin production by the surviving bacteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mechanism is preformed toxin, not ongoing production. The enterotoxin is produced in the food BEFORE ingestion; reheating kills the bacteria but cannot destroy the already-produced heat-stable toxin.

answers.text: The staphylococcal enterotoxin is heat-stable and survives 100°C for 30 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Staphylococcal enterotoxins (SE A–E) withstand 100°C for 30 minutes. Reheating kills the bacteria but the preformed toxin persists in the food, causing vomiting via vagal afferent stimulation as a superantigen.

answers.text: The thick polysaccharide capsule of S. aureus protects it from heat

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While S. aureus possesses a capsule, it does not confer heat resistance to its toxins. The critical point is that staphylococcal enterotoxins themselves are inherently heat-stable proteins resistant to boiling.

overallFeedback.feedback: Staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by preformed heat-stable enterotoxins (SE A–E) that resist 100°C for 30 minutes. Reheating destroys the bacteria but the toxin persists — this is why the dictum is 'culture the food, not the patient.'
Excellent! Staphylococcal enterotoxins are preformed in food and heat-stable — reheating kills the organism but NOT the toxin. This is why the rule is 'culture the food, not the patient.'

interactions.label: Which hepatitis B serological marker specifically indicates active viral replica

params.question: Which hepatitis B serological marker specifically indicates active viral replication and high infectivity?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HBsAg (surface antigen) indicates the presence of HBV infection — acute or chronic — but does not specifically reflect the level of viral replication. A chronic carrier may be HBsAg-positive with low replication.
Anti-HBs (surface antibody) indicates immunity — either from successful vaccination or recovery from natural infection. It is a marker of protection, not active infection or replication.

Anti-HBc IgM indicates recent acute HBV infection and is the key 'window period' marker (when HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared). It does not specifically indicate the level of viral replication.

Correct. HBeAg (e-antigen) is the soluble secreted form of the core antigen. Its presence in serum specifically indicates active viral replication with high viral load and high infectivity — critical for assessing transmission risk and guiding treatment decisions.

overallFeedback.feedback: HBeAg is the marker of active viral replication and high infectivity. Remember: HBsAg = infection present, anti-HBs = immunity, anti-HBc IgM = acute/window period, HBeAg = actively replicating and highly infectious.
Correct! HBeAg = active replication + high infectivity. Its loss (seroconversion to anti-HBe) marks a favourable turning point in chronic HBV infection.

params.question: A healthcare worker receives the complete hepatitis B vaccine series. Which serological profile confirms successful immunisation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This profile indicates active HBV infection, not successful vaccination. In a successfully vaccinated individual, the immune response produces anti-HBs antibodies; HBsAg positivity reflects viral antigen, not vaccine-derived immunity.

Correct. The recombinant HBV vaccine contains only HBsAg, so the immune response generates ONLY anti-HBs (protective level ≥10 mIU/mL). Anti-HBc is produced only during natural infection in response to core antigen and is never generated by vaccination.

Anti-HBc IgG indicates prior exposure to natural HBV infection (immune response to core antigen). The vaccine contains only HBsAg, not HBcAg, so anti-HBc is never produced by vaccination. This profile suggests past natural infection with recovery.
HBeAg indicates active viral replication in natural HBV infection and has no relation to vaccination. This profile suggests an actively replicating chronic HBV infection, not immunisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The HBV vaccine contains only recombinant HBsAg, so it generates only anti-HBs antibodies. Anti-HBc requires exposure to core antigen (natural infection only). Anti-HBs positive + anti-HBc negative = vaccine-derived immunity.
Well done! Vaccination generates ONLY anti-HBs (≥10 mIU/mL is protective). Anti-HBc is the key discriminator — its absence confirms immunity is vaccine-derived, not from natural infection.
